summary: This BCP gives implementation and operational advice for using TLS Pre-Shared Keys with RADIUS/TLS (RFC 6614) and RADIUS/DTLS (RFC 7360). It aims to ease moving from RADIUS/UDP to RADIUS/TLS.

eli5.summary: Moving to a safer way of talking with shared secrets can be bumpy. This is a how-to guide for doing it smoothly.

questions: how to move from radius udp to tls
how long should a tls psk be
should radius servers allow tls session resumption with psk
subtitle: Practical rules for replacing RADIUS shared secrets with TLS pre-shared keys without redoing the whole trust model.

tldr.problem: RADIUS/TLS and RADIUS/DTLS were specified without guidance on TLS pre-shared keys, yet many RADIUS clients cannot easily move to certificates.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC treats the PSK Identity as a replacement for the client's source IP address and the PSK as a replacement for the shared secret, and sets rules for key quality, identities, IP filtering and resumption.
tldr.outcome: Operators can move from insecure RADIUS/UDP to RADIUS/TLS in small steps, within one organization, while keeping the familiar secret-per-client workflow.

facts.label: PSK length that MUST be supported

today: RFC 9813 is a Best Current Practice published in July 2025. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it supplements RFC 6614 and RFC 7360 without changing them.

sections.title: Why TLS-PSK for RADIUS
sections.content:
RFC 6614 (RADIUS/TLS) and RFC 7360 (RADIUS/DTLS) define how (D)TLS carries RADIUS, but say nothing about TLS Pre-Shared Keys (TLS-PSKs). This RFC fills that gap. To avoid confusion it uses "shared secret" for the RADIUS shared secret and "PSK" for the TLS key.

Certificates are the usual choice, but they expire, so a working system can suddenly stop. They also need certification authorities and chains, and clients are often numerous, resource constrained and closed systems that are hard to update when a root CA expires. A PSK follows the old shared secret model, so the move to TLS can be a series of small changes.

TLS-PSK suits networks where client and server addresses are known, as with RADIUS/UDP. It does not suit clients that dynamically discover servers (RFC 7585), because there is no way to know which PSK to use with a new server. Both sides also hold the same secret, so a client could pretend to be the server, which a certificate prevents.
sections.eli5: Grown-up locks with special key cards are safer but a hassle to hand out. A secret handshake both sides already know is easier to start with, as long as you only use it among friends.

sections.title: Rules for PSKs
sections.content:
Using one PSK in both TLS 1.3 and earlier TLS versions is unsafe, so an implementation MUST NOT do it. Two different PSKs or forbidding versions below TLS 1.3 both work. RFC 9258 binds an imported PSK to the protocol version and is preferred over trust-on-first-use. Implementations must also follow RFC 9257, Section 6.

Length and quality rules: PSKs MUST be at least 16 octets and random, from a cryptographically secure source. Implementations MUST support PSKs of at least 32 octets and SHOULD support 64 octets or more. Passwords are not acceptable, and PSKs must be storable as undistinguished octets. Administrators SHOULD use at least 24 octets. The RFC shows commands such as openssl rand -base64 16 that read 128 bits (16 octets) from a secure source.

A server MUST NOT use trust-on-first-use for unknown clients; it SHOULD log the PSK Identity and source address instead. A RADIUS shared secret MUST NOT be reused as a PSK, and implementations MUST reject configuration that does so. PSK fields should be labeled "PSK" or "TLS-PSK", not "shared secret". PSK sharing across client-server relationships is NOT RECOMMENDED, and implementations MUST allow a unique PSK and identity per relationship.

PSKs SHOULD be rotated regularly, and the identity MUST change when the PSK changes. TLS-PSK MUST use modes with forward secrecy such as PSK-DH or ECDHE_PSK. Servers SHOULD invalidate credentials of clients that have not connected for a long time.
sections.eli5: A good secret is long, made by a dice-rolling machine and not by a person, and used for one pair of friends only. Change it now and then, and never reuse your old password as a new secret.

sections.title: PSK Identities
sections.content:
The PSK Identity tells the server which PSK to use. It is sent in the clear. RFC 4279 says it is UTF-8, while RFC 8446 defines it as an opaque string of 1 to 2^16-1 octets. Implementations MUST follow RFC 9257, Section 6.1.1 and the string handling of RFC 8265, and MUST support identities of 128 octets.

For privacy, the identity can be an opaque token or a Network Access Identifier whose user part is an opaque token, such as 68092112@example.com.

The identity is chosen by an untrusted client, so it must be validated before use as a lookup key. It might be invalid UTF-8, carry SQL, LDAP, REST or shell injection, or contain NUL octets. Implementations MUST validate it and either escape or reject it; rejected identities close the connection. Suggested rules: check whether it is a resumption PSK, reject identities over a fixed limit not below 128 and not above 1024, and prefer UTF-8 NAI format for administrator-configured ones. This follows a principle of discarding bad traffic quickly.

Servers MUST be able to tell external PSK Identities from TLS 1.3 session-resumption identities. One sample approach makes configured identities UTF-8 and resumption tickets non-UTF-8.
sections.eli5: The identity is the name you say at the door. Anyone can say any name, so the doorman checks that it looks sensible before looking it up in the guest book.

sections.title: Client and Server Behavior
sections.content:
Clients and servers MUST both allow a PSK for RADIUS/TLS. For TLS 1.3 they MUST support the psk_dhe_ke exchange mode and implement the recommended cipher suites in RFC 9325 and RFC 8446. A client that offered a PSK in TLS 1.3 MUST close the connection if the server did not select it. Clients MUST allow configuring a server IP address or host name, since dynamic lookup needs certificates.

A classic RADIUS/UDP server uses the source IP address as the client identity and the shared secret as proof. For TLS-PSK the PSK Identity replaces the source IP address and the PSK replaces the shared secret. The RADIUS data inside the tunnel is unchanged.

Because clients may have dynamic addresses, servers MUST perform IP address filtering. A server MUST be configurable with allowed network ranges and MUST reject connections from outside them before any PSK Identity is checked. After the handshake, it MUST NOT process application data until the client is authenticated. It then looks up the identity, closes the connection if there is no match or the address is not allowed, and verifies the PSK. Servers MUST support several PSK Identities at one source address (for example behind a NAT) and one identity at several addresses over time. A client MUST use only one authentication method, and a server supporting both PSKs and client certificates MUST accept either.
sections.eli5: The guard first checks you are coming from a street on the allowed map, then asks your name, then checks your secret. Until all that is done, nobody reads your mail.

sections.title: Where to Use It, and Resumption
sections.content:
Using TLS-PSK across unrelated organizations means sharing PSKs, which makes it easier for a client to impersonate a server. It is therefore NOT RECOMMENDED across organizational boundaries. Within one organization it is RECOMMENDED to replace RADIUS/UDP with RADIUS/TLS using TLS-PSK. There are no known security issues with using it across the public Internet. If a client is compromised, exposing a PSK lets an attacker impersonate the server as well as the client, unlike a client certificate.

Resumption is NOT RECOMMENDED for sessions that use TLS-PSK: there are few benefits and many complexities. Where allowed, systems MUST cache enough data from the full handshake to make authorization decisions on resumption, and MUST NOT resume if that data cannot be retrieved securely. Source addresses or identities may change between the original handshake and resumption, a time-of-check time-of-use problem, so decisions MUST be reevaluated. Peers MUST NOT keep resumption PSKs or tickets longer than 604800 seconds (7 days).
sections.eli5: Secret handshakes are fine inside your own club. Between different clubs they are risky, because each side knows the other's handshake.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The document points readers to Appendix E.7 of RFC 8446, RFC 9257 and RFC 9258 for the detailed TLS-PSK security considerations. These documents are newer than RFC 6614 and RFC 7360 and raise issues that were not considered in their original design.

RADIUS differs from, say, HTTPS: a broken PSK could expose credentials and personally identifiable information for many users, possibly including passwords. With forward secrecy modes such as ECDHE_PSK, attacks are limited to future sessions and historical sessions remain secure. The privacy section makes no changes to RFC 6614 and RFC 7360.
sections.eli5: One leaked secret here could let a snoop read many people's information, so locking each conversation separately matters.
